jobs.name: Overview, lexical, grammar (Parts I-III)

findings.quote:
named lifetimes, ever (`[LEX-22]`); an aliasing or exclusivity check while the program runs
(`[BRW-1]`); specialisation or higher-kinded types;
findings.question: With verdicts 152, 162 and 163 (`runtime` on a parameter, a class type, a variable), Ember stops a program while it runs because `xs` changes while `r` still looks at it. Part I still says no such check exists: I.6 lists 'an aliasing or exclusivity check while the program runs' as a non-goal, the I.4 table's row 'One name changes a place, or any number read it' says 'Checked while running: never', and PHIL-8's complete list of run-time checks has no `runtime` entry. Which is right?
findings.example:
interface Renderer:
    fn draw(ref scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]

fn render(r: runtime dyn Renderer, ref mut scratch: Array[u8]):
    frame = r.draw(scratch)
    scratch.push(owns 1)      # a `Software` renderer gave back `scratch`: the program stops here
    present(frame)
findings.why_unsettled: LT-48 (and §X.4's cost row at Hardened_11 line 5263) carry the owner's verdicts. Part I was never brought in line: PHIL-8's list ('an index in bounds, ... a disjointness test the program writes itself (`assert_disjoint`)'), the I.4 table, and I.6's non-goal all still say no view or aliasing property is ever checked while the program runs. A reader of Part I is told something the language no longer does.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: LT-48 (3716-3733), LT-1 (3550-3570), §X.4 row (5263), E3021 row (8496), H.50/H.51 changelogs (12636-12735), front matter line 28; Part I in full. JOB.md verdicts 152, 157, 162, 163.
findings.fix_idea: Add the `runtime` kind check to PHIL-8's list, give it a 'checked while running: where a value says `runtime`' cell in I.4's row, and narrow I.6's non-goal to 'no aliasing check the program did not ask for (`runtime`, `assert_disjoint`)'.

findings.quote:
Which mechanism enforces a guarantee is set per property by this specification, never by the
programmer, and it is always visible (`ember inspect --safety`) and restrictable (`@no_alias_checks`,
`[EFF-12]`).
findings.question: Does a `runtime` parameter or variable compile inside a `@no_alias_checks` function, and inside a `@nopanic(explicit)` one? What kind of RuntimeCheck does its stop record?
findings.why_unsettled: EFF-9 lists the RuntimeCheck kinds as Aliasing (only `assert_disjoint` and `check_disjoint`, 'the one run-time alias check there is'), Bounds, Stale and Arithmetic. DSJ-6 and EFF-12 repeat 'the one run-time alias check'. LT-48's check guards a read/change overlap, but it is not listed under any kind, so `@no_alias_checks` (and `ember inspect --safety`) neither forbid nor report it. The rules also do not say whether its stop counts as `Panic(Explicit)` or as an implicit panic like a bounds check.
findings.fix_idea: Classify the `runtime` compare as `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)`, since it guards an overlap, so that `@no_alias_checks` refuses it (E4030 naming the `runtime` word). Say that its stop is an implicit panic, as a bounds check's is. Then drop 'the one run-time alias check' from EFF-9 and DSJ-6.

findings.quote:
A line beginning `#!` before the first import or item is a
  directive (`[GRM-37]`), not a comment; anywhere else it is a comment.
findings.question: Is a `#!` directive written after an import a comment that is silently ignored (LEX-10, LEX-11), or `E0104` (GRM-37)?
findings.example:
import std.io
#! threads any

pub fn on_frame(dt: f32):
    io.println(f"{dt}")
findings.why_unsettled: LEX-10 makes any `#!` line after the first import or item an ordinary comment, and LEX-11 adds that a comment never affects compilation, 'including by producing a diagnostic'. GRM-37 (p03 41-42) says 'A directive after an import or item ... is `E0104`'. Under LEX-10 the program compiles with the thread contract silently not applied, which is what PHIL-12 forbids.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: LEX-10 (~411), LEX-11, GRM-37 (598-610), PHIL-12; grep '#!' across the document.
findings.fix_idea: LEX-10: a line beginning `#!` is always a directive. After the first import or item it is `E0104` (GRM-37), never a comment.

findings.quote:
Apart from
  `[LEX-23]`, a comment never affects compilation, including by producing a diagnostic.
findings.question: Does a comment line between a type-parameter line and its function compile (LEX-11), or is it `E0100` (GRM-40, verdict 154)?
findings.why_unsettled: Verdict 154 and GRM-40 ('a blank line or a comment line between `[T]` and its `fn` is `E0100` too') make a comment produce a diagnostic. LEX-11 names LEX-23 as the only exception to 'a comment never affects compilation, including by producing a diagnostic', and LEX-8 says comment-only lines affect nothing.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: LEX-8, LEX-11, LEX-11a, GRM-40 (690-709); JOB.md verdict 154.
findings.fix_idea: Add GRM-40 to LEX-11's exceptions: 'Apart from `[LEX-23]` and a comment line between a type-parameter line and its declaration (`[GRM-40]`), ...'.

findings.quote:
`E0100`: a blank line or a comment line between `[T]` and its `fn` is `E0100` too, and so is every
  line that begins with `[` anywhere else, one that begins with a list included (`[10, 20].len()` on a
findings.question: Does a `match` arm whose pattern is a list pattern compile? Its line begins with `[` and the next line is not a function, struct or class, so GRM-40 (verdict 155) makes it `E0100`, while `primary_pattern` produces `[p, q, ..rest]`.
findings.why_unsettled: The pattern grammar (p03 496) offers list patterns, and only a match arm can start a line with one (`for` lines start with `for`). GRM-40's 'every line that begins with `[`' refuses every such arm, in both the statement form (`[a, b]:`) and the expression form (`[a, b] => ...`). The verdict was put to the owner with expression lines (`[10, 20].len()`), not patterns. No other rule describes list patterns.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: GRM-40 (690-709), III.6 patterns (1053-1090), CTL-5, ENM-2; grep for slice or list patterns in examples (none found); JOB.md verdicts 154, 155.
findings.fix_idea: Limit GRM-40's catch-all to lines where an item or a statement begins: inside a `match`'s arm list a line beginning `[` is an arm's pattern. Or, if the owner prefers, remove list patterns from the grammar.

findings.question: Is `setup(shares mut game)` for `fn setup(owns game: shares mut Game)` accepted (verdict 160), or `E3028` because GRM-15 requires `owns` before every argument for an `owns` parameter 'whatever is given'? The same question for `ROSTER.push(weakref this)` and for a constructor argument `Words(names=xs)` (verdict 159).

findings.searched: Hardened_11: GRM-15 (955-972), FN-2a (2076-2100), OWN-9 (3102-3112), BRW/OWN-13 (3155-3163), H.50 (12636-12648); grep 'setup(shares mut game)', 'ROSTER.push(weakref this)', 'owns shares', 'owns weakref'. JOB.md verdicts 147, 149, 159, 160.
findings.fix_idea: In GRM-15 and FN-2a, after 'whatever is given', add the exceptions: a value made in the call with `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` or `weakref` takes no `owns` (verdict 160), and a constructor's argument works as `=` does (verdict 159).

findings.quote:
*Note.* `Emitter("fountain")` passes a string literal where a `String` is expected; the literal
allocates the `String` there (`[TXT-9]`), and `owns name` takes it over.
findings.question: For a class whose written `init` has an `owns` parameter, is the call `Emitter(label)` or `Emitter(owns label)`? And for an `init` with a plain parameter (`fn init(name: String)`, which E2108's help suggests), does `Emitter(label)` hand `label` over, as `=` does, or only lend it?
findings.why_unsettled: Verdict 159 was decided on a memberwise constructor (`Words(names=xs)`): 'a constructor's argument takes no word: it works as `=` does'. FN-2a and OWN-9 say the same for every constructor. But a written `init` is a function with its own parameter words, and GRM-15 and FN-2a require `owns` before an argument for an `owns` parameter. Neither rule says which wins for `init`. With a plain `init` parameter, the 'as `=`' reading hands over a value the function only reads. I.5's example depends on the answer.
findings.fix_idea: Say that a memberwise constructor's arguments work as `=` (verdict 159), and that a written `init` is called with its parameters' words like any function (`Emitter(owns label)`). Then I.5 writes `Emitter(owns "fountain")`, or the owner rules otherwise.

findings.quote:
* `[GRM-29]` *(new in 0.9.9)* An `expr_list` of two or more expressions, or of one expression followed by a comma, is a
  tuple: `a, b = b, a` swaps, and `return x, y` returns a tuple.
findings.question: Does `last = (frame,)` or `return pos,` compile, and if so what is its type? GRM-29, GRM-38 ('`(e,)` a tuple'), `tuple_lit` and `tuple_type` (`(int,)`) make one-element tuples, while TYP-27 says 'a tuple type has two or more elements' (ODR-071).
findings.example:
fn snapshot(frame: int) -> (int, int):
    return frame,          # a trailing comma: a 1-tuple by GRM-29, a type TYP-27 says does not exist
findings.why_unsettled: Part III produces one-element tuple values and types; TYP-27 refuses the type. Verdict 115 itself calls `(A,)` 'a tuple `[TYP-27]` refuses'. No rule says what happens to `x = e,` or `(e,)`.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: TYP-27 (1147-1149), GRM-29, GRM-38, tuple_type/tuple_lit; JOB.md verdict 115.
findings.fix_idea: Follow TYP-27: one expression with a trailing comma, `(e,)` and `(T,)` are refused (E0100, help: remove the comma). GRM-29 and GRM-38 drop the one-element form.

findings.quote:
`import x as y`. The name is declared there with its words, as a pattern name is (`[GRM-13]`):
  plain `p` is a read-only view and never changes (`E3023`); `if ui exists as ref mut me:` may change
findings.question: When `exists as` opens a temporary `Option` (the result of `pop()` or `remove()`), may the opened name be handed over (`done.push(owns job)`)? How long does the temporary live? `for` over a temporary hands each element to the loop's name (CTL-1), but an opened name is only a read-only view and `opened_name` has no `owns` word.
findings.why_unsettled: GRM-44, CTL-11 and BRW-14 make every plain opened name a view that keeps its place, and `name_word` offers only `ref`, `ref mut` and `copy of`. CTL-1 says a temporary given to `for` is handed over with no word. `match` needs `owns` before its scrutinee, but `Some(...)` may not stand in a `while` header (GRM-19). So a queue-draining loop either cannot be written in the header form or has an unstated meaning, and the temporary's lifetime is not stated either.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: GRM-44, GRM-19, GRM-13, CTL-1 (2651-2666), CTL-11 (2709-2715), BRW-14, OWN-10/OWN-11 (3118-3135); grep 'exists as' (all uses: links and map lookups only, none on a temporary), 'pop() exists as', 'exists as owns'.
findings.fix_idea: As in CTL-1: when the value opened is a temporary, it is handed over and the plain opened name owns what it holds; a place opened stays a view. Otherwise add `owns` to `name_word`.

findings.quote: name_word     := "ref" ["mut"] | "copy" "of"
findings.question: Does `for copy of e in enemies:` or the match arm `Some(copy of v):` compile? A name after `exists as` may take `copy of` (verdicts 66 and 67), but loop and pattern names, which GRM-42 treats as the same kind of list, have only `ref` and `ref mut` (`primary_pattern := ... | "ref" ["mut"] IDENT`).
findings.example:
for copy of e in enemies:
    e.hp -= 10                  # a preview on a copy of each enemy
    preview.push(owns e)

match scores.get(name):
    Some(copy of v):
        v += 1
    None:
        pass
findings.why_unsettled: GRM-42 says loop names, pattern names and the names after `exists as` follow one rule for words. BRW-14 makes `exists as copy of v` 'the one exception' that may be changed. No reason is given why the same word is refused on a loop or pattern name; the match form of the very same map lookup cannot say it.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: GRM-42, GRM-44, BRW-12/BRW-14/BRW-15 (3206-3260), CTL-1, E3023 row; grep 'for copy of', 'copy of v):'; JOB.md verdicts 66, 67, 95.
findings.fix_idea: Add `"copy" "of" IDENT` to `primary_pattern` (so loop names and match arms take it), with BRW-14's exception widened to every name declared `copy of`.

findings.quote: field_decl    := ["let"] IDENT ":" type ["from" (IDENT | "static")] ["guarded" "by" IDENT]
findings.question: Where does `runtime` go when the value whose kind is known only while running is a field (`this.renderer`), a lambda's typed parameter, or a type with a word before it (`owns dyn Renderer`, `ref A`)? `runtime` is allowed on parameters and variables only, 'before a `dyn` or class type'.
findings.example:
class Scene:
    renderer: owns dyn Renderer
    scratch: Array[u8] = []

    fn render():
        frame = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)
        this.scratch.push(owns 1)   # E3021, help: `runtime` on the parameter or the variable: there is neither
        present(frame)

fn show(owns p: runtime owns dyn Picker):   # or `owns runtime dyn Picker`, or refused?
    pass
findings.why_unsettled: LT-48 and the grammar give `runtime` to `param` and `var_decl` only, not to `field_decl`, `lambda_param` or `fn_type_param`. A method using a `dyn` field cannot be written with the check: copying the field into a local would hand it over, and taking a part out of a class object is refused (OWN-11). 'Before a `dyn` or class type' does not say whether `owns dyn I`, `shares mut A` or `ref dyn I` counts. The brief's own example of an inconsistency is a word allowed on parameters but not on fields.
findings.fix_idea: Allow `runtime` right after the `:` of a field (guarding each line that uses the field) and of a typed lambda parameter, as on a parameter. State that it goes before the type's words (`owns p: runtime owns dyn Picker`).

findings.quote: unary         := ("-" | "~") unary | value_word unary | "cast" postfix_expr "as" type | power
findings.question: Does `xs.iter().filter(owns fn(x: int) -> bool: x % 2 == 0)` parse? The grammar puts a lambda at `expression` level only. `value_word unary` cannot reach a lambda (`atom` has none), so `owns fn(...)` is not produced, although GRM-15, FN-2a and verdict 158 require it. It is also unstated how far `owns` reaches over a lambda whose body 'extends as far right as possible' (`owns fn(x) => x * 2`).
findings.why_unsettled: Part III says every construct used anywhere appears in it, and that an example it does not produce is a defect. `owns fn` appears in I.5, GRM-15, FN-2a, STD-19 and LT-48's neighbourhood (Hardened_11 344, 962, 2082, 5443). The binding rule 'owns binds as `-` does' (verdict 161) gives no answer for a lambda operand.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: grammar expressions (889-935), precedence table (865-886), GRM-15, GRM-17, GRM-43, FN-2a; grep 'owns fn('. JOB.md verdicts 158, 161.
findings.fix_idea: `unary := value_word (lambda | unary) | ...`, with `owns` before a lambda covering the whole lambda, whose body extends as far right as possible, as at level 2.

findings.quote: bound_list    := type {"+" type}                        -- after `dyn` and `some` only
findings.question: Are several interfaces after `dyn` or `some` still joined with `+` (`owns dyn Shape + Debug`), when TYP-17 (verdicts 109 to 112) makes 'needs joined with `+`' an `E0100` everywhere else a list of needs is written?
findings.why_unsettled: Verdict 109: 'The same spelling goes everywhere a list of needs is written'. 110-112 extend it to interface parents, `extend` and associated types. The `dyn` and `some` lists keep Rust's `+`, with no reason given, and no example in the specification uses either form.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: TYP-17 (1543-1553), TYP-32, GRM-31, bound_list (638, 737); grep for `dyn ... +` and `some ... +` (none). JOB.md 109-112.
findings.fix_idea: Write several bounds after `dyn` and `some` as `needs` does, in round brackets (`owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`), and refuse `+` there with E0100 as in TYP-17. Or record why `+` stays.

findings.quote: (lexed as keywords so that no program uses them as names; any use is `E1010`,
findings.question: Can a C struct field or function named `owned`, `self`, `async`, `await` or `macro` be imported and used as `r#owned` or `r#self`? LEX-14 lets `r#name` use 'a keyword' and the FFI table maps 'an identifier that is an Ember keyword' to a raw identifier, but these words are listed apart from the 52 keywords and 'any use' of `owned` and `self` is E1010.
findings.why_unsettled: LEX-14 speaks of 'any keyword of the table below' (the 52). LEX-15's reserved-for-future words and its 'reserved and not words of Ember' (`owned`, `self`) are outside that table. Whether `r#` lifts them is not said, and C headers do use `owned` as a field name and `self` as a parameter name.
findings.searched: Hardened_11: LEX-14 (437-440), LEX-15 (455-478), FFI C-to-Ember table row (7105), E0005/E1010 rows; grep 'r#'.
findings.fix_idea: Say that `r#` gives a name for any lexed keyword, the reserved and removed words included (`r#owned`, `r#self`). E1010 then applies to the bare word only.

findings.quote: | "[" expr_list "]" | "." IDENT | "." INT
findings.question: Does `edge.0.1` (element 1 of element 0 of a nested tuple) parse? Maximal munch lexes `0.1` as one FLOAT, so the postfix `"." INT` never sees `0` and `1`.
findings.example:
fn first_end(edges: Span[((int, int), (int, int))]) -> int:
    return edges[0].0.1
findings.why_unsettled: LEX-18 decides only `1.` followed by an identifier character and `1.0`. Nothing says the lexer splits `0.1` after a `.`, which nested tuple access needs (Rust had to special-case it).
findings.searched: Hardened_11: LEX-18, LEX-21, float_lit grammar, postfix grammar; grep for `.N.N` access (none).
findings.fix_idea: LEX-18: directly after a `.` token, a digit sequence is lexed as an INT only, so `t.0.1` is `(t.0).1`.

findings.quote: file          := {directive} {NEWLINE} {import_decl} {item}
findings.question: Does an entry-file script parse? GRM-2 and FN-8 allow statements at file scope ('items anywhere in the file'), but the `file` production, in what Part III calls the complete grammar, admits only items after the imports.
findings.example:
import std.io

fn greet(name: StrView) -> String:
    return f"hello {name}"

io.println(greet("world"))
findings.why_unsettled: FN-8 settles what the statements mean (source order, implicit `main`, interleaved with items). The grammar that is declared complete cannot produce them.
findings.fix_idea: `file := {directive} {NEWLINE} {import_decl} {item | statement}`, with statements permitted only in the entry file (GRM-2).

jobs.notes:
I read Parts I to III in full and checked every rule against Hardened_11 and JOB.md. Patterns and points for the other reviewers:

(1) Verdicts 152, 162 and 163 (`runtime`) reached LT-48, §X.4 and E3021, but not the parts that describe run-time checks in general: Part I's PHIL-8, I.4 and I.6, and EFF-9, EFF-12 and DSJ-6 in Part X, which still say `assert_disjoint` is 'the one run-time alias check'. The Part X reviewer should take J1-02 further.

(2) Verdicts 159 and 160 live in FN-2a and OWN-9 (159 only) and in the H.50 changelog. GRM-15's list of where `owns` is required has no exceptions, and no rule text carries 160. The Part VI/VII reviewer should check FN-2a for 160.

(3) Verdict 163's own line uses `Box[dyn Renderer]`/`Box(Gpu(...))`. LT-48 writes it as `p: runtime dyn Picker = ...`, a local of bare `dyn Picker` type holding a struct (`Mine(items=[9])`) by value. Whether a `dyn I` local or parameter without `owns` holds an unsized struct value inline, and who owns it, is for the TYP-45/OBJ-2 reviewer (OBJ-2 says a `dyn I` of a class object is one pointer, which says nothing of structs).

(4) FN-2a and verdict 150 lend a function from a variable to a standard-library function with no word, but a program's own function with the same `owns f: F` parameter takes `owns h`. That is the owner's verdict, but it is a library-only path; the STD/CLO reviewer may want to confirm it is intended.

(5) CLS-2's E2108 help ('write `fn init(name: String):`') suggests an init whose `this.name = name` stores a read-only view into an owning field. This is linked to J1-07; the message wording is the lead's.

Checked and settled, so not reported: GRM-4 against verdict 42 re-pointing (settled by BRW-13); SPN-1's `ref mut` Array to MutSpan re-pointing (settled); the overlay grammar (separate, GRM-35); GRM-8a; precedence of `**`, `using` and `as`; GRM-12 against ENM-1 for unqualified variants (ENM-1 settles it); `static fn` in interfaces (used in std); generator allocation (CORO-5).

Considered and dropped as too weak: `where` clauses missing from GRM-41's first-line order; `static` (not `mut`) with `guarded by` allowed by the grammar but not by GRM-46; `shader` called 'reserved' in I.6 but absent from LEX-15; `gen` lambdas (GRM-21 'wherever fn is'); `int_suffix` not attached to `int_lit` (a typo); a `match` expression inside brackets (impossible under LEX-6, but no example needs it); `if None = x:`.

jobs.name: Types (Part IV)

findings.quote: `copy of x` makes a value with `Clone` (`[OWN-8]`), and every `Copy` type is `Clone`; before what it cannot copy as itself (a `weakref` link, a value of a view type, a type with no `Clone`) it is `E2116`.
findings.question: Does `copy of` compile for a `StrView`, a `Span[T]`, or a `@derive(Copy)` struct holding a `StrView`? If it does, is the result a view (Clone of StrView returns Self) or text of your own?
findings.example:
@derive(Copy)
struct Token:
    text: StrView
    line: int

fn main():
    src = String("let x = 1")
    tok = Token(text=src.as_str(), line=1)
    t2 = copy of tok          # STR-3 / verdict 68: works on every Copy struct; OWN-8: E2116, a view type
    w = src.as_str()
    w2 = copy of w            # TYP-36 table: StrView is Clone and Copy; OWN-8: E2116 "to make your own copy write String(w)"
    println(t2.line, w2)
findings.why_unsettled: Verdict 68 ("A `Copy` type always works with `copy of`") and OWN-8's own sentence "Every `Copy` type has `Clone` ... so `b = copy of a` works" accept it. The marker table says `StrView` and `Span` are always `Copy`, and the TYP-36 table gives `StrView` Clone. But OWN-8's E2116 list names `StrView` and `Span[T]` outright, and TYP-36 refuses "a value of a view type", which takes in any `@derive(Copy)` struct holding a `ref T` or `StrView`. STR-3 says "`copy of` works on every `Copy` struct". Verdict 10 (the copy word copies the thing itself, never a link) would make `copy of w` give a `String`, which no rule says either.
findings.searched: OWN-7, OWN-8 (spec 3172-3199), STR-3 (2193-2198), E2116 row (8449), marker table (1666), TYP-36 table; JOB.md verdicts 10, 12, 68, 79, 93.
findings.fix_idea: Decide one meaning. Either `copy of` before a view copies what it views (`String`, an `Array`), as verdict 10 and `.copy_each()` do, and the `Clone` rows for views are fixed to match. Or `Copy` views and `Copy` view structs copy their bits as verdict 68 says, and the E2116 bullet keeps only non-`Copy` views (`ref mut`, `MutSpan`).

findings.quote: It may follow an `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` type, a class type, or an `Array`, a `Map` or a `Set`; after any other type it is `E2114`
findings.question: Does `name: String using LevelArena` compile, and do `Deque`, `SmallArray` and the other heap collections take `using`?
findings.why_unsettled: IV.1's Collection row says `Array`, `String`, `Map`, `Set`, ... take their heap buffer "from the memory manager its type names (`[TYP-46]`)". ALC-1 says "a value that grows (an `Array`, `Map`, `Set` or `String`) made in it keeps the word", so a `String` can be made in a manager. Yet TYP-46's and ALC-1's closed lists leave out `String` (and `Deque`, `SmallArray`), and say anything else is `E2114`.
findings.searched: TYP-46, ALC-1 (spec 4606-4635), ALC-2, STD-7, the collections section 6579-6610, PHIL-2; grep `String.*using`, `new_in`; JOB.md verdicts 19, 24, 47, 107.
findings.fix_idea: State the rule by property, as TYP-46's first sentence does ("a type whose value has heap memory of its own"): every standard heap collection, `String` included, takes `using`. Make the list of examples illustrative rather than closed.

findings.quote: `dyn I` alone is a parameter's type, a read-only view of the value (`ref mut v: dyn I` may change it).
findings.question: Does a local `p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])` compile, and who owns the `Mine` it holds?
findings.example:
fn main():
    xs = [1, 2]
    p: runtime dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])
    r = p.pick(xs)
    xs.push(owns 3)
    println(r)
findings.why_unsettled: TYP-45 and IV.9 allow plain `dyn I` only as a parameter's type, a view (`ref dyn I`), or held as `owns`/`shares`/`shares mut dyn I`. A bare interface elsewhere is refused (E2173's family). Yet LT-48 (spec 3720, 3729) and `[LT-1]` (3563) use a local of type `dyn Picker` initialised from temporaries, which nothing owns. Verdict 163's own line was `renderer: runtime Box[dyn Renderer] = Box(Gpu(...)) ...`, an owning value, which TYP-45's spelling makes `owns dyn Renderer`. The spec carries it as a bare `dyn` local instead.
findings.searched: TYP-45, IV.9, LT-48 (spec 3716-3733), LT-1 (3560-3567), E2173; decisions.md N39; JOB.md verdicts 152, 162, 163.
findings.fix_idea: Write the local as `p: runtime owns dyn Picker = owns Mine(items=[9]) if ... else owns Yours(items=[9])`, as TYP-45 spells an owned interface value. Or add to TYP-45 that a local may be `dyn I` and say what owns its value.

findings.quote: A type has an operator only by implementing its interface (`[TYP-40]`); a method that merely shares the name is not one. ... `bool`, `char` and `String` implement none of them (`String`'s `+` takes its left operand over, `[TXT-11]`).
findings.question: Is `String`'s `+` (and `s += t`) an `Add`/`AddAssign` implementation or not? Does a generic function bounded by `Add` accept a `String`?
findings.example:
[T: needs Add[StrView, Output = T]]
fn suffix(owns a: T, b: StrView) -> T:
    return a + b

fn main():
    s = String("hp: ")
    s += "10"                    # TXT-11: appends
    t = s + "!"                 # TXT-11: takes `s` over
    u = suffix(owns t, "?")     # TYP-21: String implements no Add, so E2040?
    println(u)
findings.why_unsettled: TYP-21 says an operator exists only through its interface, and in the same rule that `String` implements none of the operator interfaces. TXT-11 then gives `String` a `+` and a `+=`. So either `String` has an operator by a path no interface declares (the hidden special path the owner's checklist forbids), or it implements `Add` and TYP-21's sentence is wrong. With `+` built in, a `String` fails `Add` bounds while `a + b` on it compiles.
findings.searched: TYP-21, TYP-40, TXT-11 (spec 6520-6530), the standard-interface sketch, STD-*; docs/OWNER-DIRECTION.md principle on hidden special paths; JOB.md verdict 84/145 (one rule for every type).
findings.fix_idea: Make `String` implement `Add[StrView, Output = String]` (its `add` written `owns this`) and `AddAssign[StrView]`, and drop `String` from TYP-21's "implement none" list. Its `+` then goes through TYP-21 like every other operator.

findings.quote:
Each rule composes with the others only where stated (widening after range erasure, and rule 11
  after rules 1–4).
findings.question: Does `return x` compile in a function returning `Option[int]` when `x` is a loop name, i.e. a read-only view (rule 7, then rule 11)? Does `y: Option[u64] = n` compile after `n = 5` (rule 12, then 11)? Does `best: Option[Entity] = player` compile for a subclass (rule 8 upcast, then 11)?
findings.why_unsettled: Read literally, the composition clause refuses these programs: rule 11 composes only after rules 1-4. But rule 12 (known-number widening) is the same act as rule 1, and rule 7 (reading through a view) is what every `for` loop name needs. So `y: u64 = n` is accepted while `y: Option[u64] = n` is refused. And `return w` works for an `-> int` function but not for `-> Option[int]`. No reason is given for leaving 7, 8 and 12 out.
findings.searched: TYP-5 (spec 1160-1192), TYP-23 (rule 11 after `x = None`), CTL-1 (loop names are read-only views, 2650-2665), TYP-14, RNG-2; JOB.md (no verdict on composition).
findings.fix_idea: Let rule 11 apply after rules 1-4, 7, 8 and 12, the one-level limit unchanged, so wrapping in `Some` follows whatever conversion the plain type would get.

findings.quote: `ref T` and `Span[T]` are when `T` is `ThreadShared`, `ref mut T` and `MutSpan[T]` when `T` is `Send`
findings.question: Is a `sharedref mut T` link, or a struct holding one, `Send`? Is it `ThreadShared`? Does `[T: needs Send]` accept a `Watcher`, and does `thread_shared` accept one inside it?
findings.example:
class Player:
    hp: int = 10

struct Watcher:
    target: sharedref mut Player

[T: needs Send]
fn hand_off(owns item: T, tx: Sender[T]):
    tx.send(owns item).expect("gone")

fn main():
    p = Player()
    w = Watcher(target=sharedref mut p)
    tx, rx = channel[Watcher](capacity=1)
    hand_off(owns w, tx)       # Send by THR-8's list, or refused?
    p.hp -= 1                  # the other thread may write p.hp through its holder
findings.why_unsettled: THR-8's and the marker table's lists of what is not `Send` name `shares`, `shares mut`, a `weakref` to one, and thread-bound values, but never `sharedref mut`. THR-9's list of what is not `ThreadShared` leaves it out too. Inferred structurally, `Watcher` would be `Send` and `ThreadShared`, which allows a data race through the other holders on this thread. THR-13's last bullet says only that "an unscoped thread never holds one (E7015)"; the markers, which bounds and `thread_shared` read, say nothing.
findings.fix_idea: Add `sharedref mut T` to THR-8's one-thread list (not `Send`, as `shares mut`) and to THR-9's "are not" list, keeping the scoped-task reduction of verdict 77 as THR-13 states it.

findings.quote:
`...` after a type parameter's name makes it a **pack**: any number of types, none
  included (`[Cs...]` above `fn view() -> View[Cs...]:`).
findings.question: Can a struct or class take a pack (`[Ts...]` above `struct Event:`), and what may its body write? A field holding the pack's values, a function type `fn(Ts...)`, a tuple type `(Ts...)`, or a per-type expansion such as `ref Pool[Cs]...`?
findings.why_unsettled: Verdict 115 says "a function or type takes any number of types". It names among the uses "a tuple's interfaces written once for every size", `zip` over any number of iterators (a tuple item), the ECS `View[Cs...]` (one pool per type), and "`Event[int, String]` with handlers `fn(int, String)`". TYP-47 defines a pack only on a function: its last parameter, `Cs...` among type arguments, `values...` in a call, and `for v in values`. It does not say whether a pack may appear in a function type, a tuple type or a field, or how one type is expanded per element. A tuple of a pack with zero or one types would also meet TYP-27's "a tuple type has two or more elements".
findings.searched: TYP-47 (spec 1585-1600), TYP-27, TYP-19, ECS-3/ECS-4 (6067-6090), STD-26 (zip), STD-9, the 0.9.15 change log (12367-12369); decisions.md section 7 rows 145-147; JOB.md verdicts 115-117.
findings.fix_idea: Following C++ (verdict 116), allow a pack in function types (`fn(Ts...)`), tuple types (`(Ts...)`, with zero and one element allowed for a pack), and pattern expansion (`ref Pool[Cs]...`) in fields and type arguments, and say how TYP-27's two-element rule treats a pack tuple.

findings.quote:
An interface is usable as `dyn` only if every method has an object
  (none is a `static fn`), does not return `Self` by value (methods marked `where Self: needs Sized`
  excepted), and is not generic
findings.question: Is an interface whose method takes another `Self` (`fn hits(other: Self) -> bool`) usable as `dyn`, and if so, what does the call do when the two values are of different kinds? Is `owns dyn I` `Ord` when `I` requires `Ord`?
findings.example:
interface Collider:
    fn hits(other: Self) -> bool

struct Circle implements Collider:
    r: float
    fn hits(other: Circle) -> bool:
        return this.r + other.r > 1.0

struct Box2 implements Collider:
    w: float
    fn hits(other: Box2) -> bool:
        return this.w + other.w > 1.0

fn check(a: dyn Collider, b: dyn Collider) -> bool:
    return a.hits(b)              # compiles? a Circle given a Box2?

fn main():
    println(check(Circle(r=0.5), Box2(w=2.0)))
findings.why_unsettled: TYP-22 forbids only static methods, returning `Self` by value, and generic methods, so a `Self`-typed parameter passes its test. Nothing says what `a.hits(b)` does when `b` is another kind: refused when compiling, stopped while running, or false. TYP-36 settles this only for `Eq` ("values of two different kinds are never equal", a method-table entry) and is silent on `Ord`. So `sorted(shapes)` over `Array[owns dyn Shape]` with `interface Shape: needs Ord:` is undecided too.
findings.searched: TYP-22, TYP-36 (owns dyn Eq/Clone), TYP-44, IV.9, DSP-4/DSP-6; grep `other: Self` (only Eq and Ord in the sketch); JOB.md (no verdict).
findings.fix_idea: Add to TYP-22: a method with a `Self`-typed parameter makes the interface not usable as `dyn` (E2050) unless marked `where Self: needs Sized`. Keep `Eq` (and state `Ord`, ordering kinds by type index) as the method-table entries TYP-36 names.

findings.quote:
A reference, and an `owns T`, is read through wherever a `T` is wanted —
  a field access, a method call, an operand, an argument to a plain parameter.
findings.question: Is a `shares T`, `shares mut T` or `thread_shared T` value read through as a `T` for an argument to a plain parameter or an operand? Does it implement `Display`, `Eq` and `Hash` as `T` does (`println(other)`, `a == b`)?
findings.why_unsettled: TYP-14 and TYP-5 rule 7 name only `ref`/views and `owns T` as read through. IV.11 strips one level of `shares`/`shares mut`/`thread_shared` only for method calls, and the IV.6a example reads fields through them (`reader.hp`). TYP-36 and TYP-39 give `ref T` and `owns T` the interfaces of `T`, but say nothing of shared owners. So whether a shared list can be passed to a reading function, printed, compared or used as a map key is not decided. Class objects (identity `==`) and shared values of structs and collections may need different answers.
findings.searched: TYP-14, TYP-5, TYP-36, TYP-39, IV.11, RC-1, RC-2a (`x: shares T` parameters), OWN-13, FN-1; grep for shares with Display/==/Hash; JOB.md verdicts 4, 23, 32.
findings.fix_idea: Extend TYP-14 and rule 7 to every owner word (`shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`) as IV.11 already does for methods. Give them TYP-36's `ref T` line (`Eq`, `Ord`, `Hash`, `Display`, `Debug` as `T` does), keeping class objects' identity `==`.

findings.quote:
`cast s as Circle`
  gives the `Circle`, on `owns dyn` and `shares dyn` values too, ... A cast of a place is a place: the name bound from it is read-only
  unless written `ref mut`
findings.question: How does a program take an `owns Circle` out of an `owns dyn Shape` (Rust's `Box::downcast`), or make one more `shares Circle` owner from a `shares dyn Shape`? What is the type of `cast` applied to a temporary?
findings.why_unsettled: TYP-44 and DSP-6 say a cast of a place is a place, bound read-only or `ref mut`, but never as a hand-over. So no line takes ownership of the concrete value out of an `owns dyn` or `shares dyn`. Whether `owns cast s as Circle`, `shares cast s as Circle`, or a cast of a temporary (`cast shapes.pop().unwrap() as Circle`) is allowed, and what type it gives, is not said.
findings.searched: TYP-44, DSP-4, DSP-6 (spec 4209-4231), OWN-13, ERR-8 (`downcast_ref` only), §II operator table (2592); grep `owns cast`, `downcast`; JOB.md verdicts 25, 27.
findings.fix_idea: Let the value words compose with `cast`, as they do before any value (OWN-13): `c = owns cast s as Circle` hands `s` over as an `owns Circle`, and `shares cast s as Circle` makes one more owner. A cast of a temporary gives the value, held as the cast operand's word says.

findings.quote:
`ref_to_ptr(r: T) -> *T` and `ref_to_ptr(ref mut r: T) -> *mut T`, called
`ref_to_ptr(x)` and `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)`
findings.question: Are there two functions named `ref_to_ptr`, chosen by the word at the call? If so, how does that fit 'There is no overloading', and may a program write the same pair itself?
findings.why_unsettled: TYP-26: "two functions of one name in one scope are `E1030`, except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types". IV.5 declares two `ref_to_ptr` that differ only in the parameter's word and the result type. It falls under neither exception, so either the library has an overload a program cannot write (a hidden special path), or the pair is one function whose result depends on the call's word, which no rule describes.
findings.searched: IV.5, TYP-26, TYP-7, FFI section (spec 7341), ODR-075 row (10609); grep `ref_to_ptr`; JOB.md (no verdict; verdict 117 removed the last compiler-known special functions).
findings.fix_idea: Use two names (`ref_to_ptr(r)` and `ref_to_mut_ptr(ref mut r)`), or let `r as *T` / `r as *mut T` (already safe) be the one spelling, so TYP-26 holds with no exception.

findings.quote:
A program writes `Send` by
  hand, for a struct or enum of its own package that holds a raw pointer, only as `unsafe extend T
  implements Send:`
findings.question: May a class that holds a raw pointer (a wrapper of a foreign handle) be declared `Send` with `unsafe extend`?
findings.example:
class GpuTexture:
    handle: *mut u8
    size: int

# SAFETY: the driver's texture handles may be used from any thread
unsafe extend GpuTexture implements Send:
    pass

fn main():
    tex = GpuTexture(handle=null[*mut u8](), size=0)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tex: tex.size)
    println(h.join())
findings.why_unsettled: TYP-43 limits the hand-written `unsafe extend ... implements Send` to "a struct or enum". THR-8 says "the author of a type that holds a raw pointer declares it with `unsafe extend T implements Send:`", and calls a class object `Send` when its fields are. So a class wrapping a C handle is either never `Send` (a struct may be, its class sibling may not, with no reason given) or allowed by THR-8 against TYP-43.
findings.searched: TYP-43, marker table, THR-8 (spec 5368-5383), UNS-*, E3100 row (8514); JOB.md verdicts 60, 114.
findings.fix_idea: Say "a struct, enum or class of its own package" in TYP-43, matching THR-8's "a type".

findings.quote:
`weakref T`: a link that does not keep its target alive and may hold none (`parent: weakref Node
    = None`)
findings.question: Is `Option[weakref Node]` a legal type, distinct from `weakref Node = None`? If so, does `if n.next exists as w:` give a link that must be opened a second time?
findings.example:
class Node:
    name: String
    next: Option[weakref Node] = None    # E3032's help writes this
    prev: weakref Node = None            # TYP-45 / WK-11 write this

fn walk(n: Node):
    if n.next exists as w:               # `w` a Node view, or a weakref still to open?
        println(w.name)
findings.why_unsettled: TYP-45 and WK-11 make an empty link `weakref T = None`, a link that may hold none and is opened with `exists as`. WK-6's E3032 message and the B17 table row tell the programmer to write `next: Option[weakref Node]`, a second spelling for the same thing. Neither rule says whether an `Option` of a link is allowed, refused, or opened in one step or two (TYP-5 rule 11 avoids `Option[Option[T]]`, but a link is not an `Option`).
findings.searched: TYP-45, WK-11 (spec 4244-4258), WK-6 (4359-4366), B17 row (8239), GRM-44 (832-851), TYP-13; grep `Option[weakref`; JOB.md verdicts 9, 99 (whose line was `Option[weakref Node]`).
findings.fix_idea: Keep one spelling: `weakref Node = None`, and change E3032's help to it. Either refuse `Option[weakref T]` with a message giving that line, or define that `exists as` opens both levels.

findings.quote:
one of several owners of such a value, reading it or changing it too; `dyn I` as a parameter's type is a
  read-only view (`ref mut v: dyn I` may change it).
findings.question: Does a local declared `p: dyn Picker = Mine(...) if ... else Yours(...)` compile, and who owns and ends the value made on that line?
findings.example:
interface Renderer:
    fn draw(frame: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]

fn main():
    renderer: dyn Renderer = Gpu(pixels=[0]) if input() == "gpu" else Software(unused=0)
    scratch = [0u8]
    frame = renderer.draw(scratch)
    println(frame)
findings.why_unsettled: IFC-5 and TYP-45 say `dyn I` alone is a parameter's type only, a read-only view, and that a value held alone is `owns dyn I`. LT-1 and LT-48 (which carry verdicts 152 and 163) use `p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])` as a local that holds a value made right there. Verdict 163's own line was `Box[dyn Renderer]`, which is `owns dyn` in 0.9.15. So either this local is illegal (and the LT examples are wrong), or `dyn I` is a local type with no rule saying who owns the value or when it ends (owner, or a view of a temporary that ends with the line?).
findings.searched: Spec: TYP-45 (line 1503: "`dyn I` alone is a parameter's type"), LT-1 (3563), LT-48 (3716-3730), var_decl grammar (770, `runtime` before a dyn or class type), grep for `: dyn ... =` and `Box[dyn`; JOB verdicts 152, 163; decisions N39.
findings.fix_idea: Keep TYP-45's one rule: a local that holds the value says who owns it, `p: runtime owns dyn Picker = owns Mine(items=[9]) if ... else owns Yours(items=[9])`, and respell LT-1/LT-48's examples that way. A bare `dyn I` stays a parameter's view.

findings.quote:
and may be passed by its name, so a long lambda may be written inside the call
  (`a = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared log: log.push("a"))`) or as a local function
  (`fn push_a() thread_shared log:` with the body `log.push("a")`, then `a = thread.spawn(push_a)`).
findings.question: Is `thread.spawn(push_a)` (a local function with state, passed by name) a hand-over with no word, a loan, or E3028? Can `push_a()` still be called after it?
findings.example:
import std.thread

fn main():
    log = thread_shared Log()
    fn push_a() thread_shared log:
        log.push("a")
    a = thread.spawn(push_a)
    push_a()
    a.join()
findings.why_unsettled: THR-10 declares `spawn(owns f: thread_shared fn() -> R)`, and the thread may outlive its maker. GRM-15 says an argument for an `owns` parameter takes `owns`, whatever is given (E3028 without it). FN-2a says a function from a variable given to a standard-library function is lent and takes no word. CLO-12 and GRM-28 show `thread.spawn(push_a)` with no word. Lending to a thread that outlives the caller is impossible, `push_a` holds state and is not `Copy` (CLO-10), and no rule makes the bare form a hand-over.
findings.fix_idea: Limit FN-2a's loan to a standard-library parameter that runs the function only during the call (the CLO-14 consumers). A function kept past the call is handed over as GRM-15 says: `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`. Respell CLO-12 and GRM-28 that way.

findings.quote:
value over as `=` does (`[OWN-9]`). A function from a variable given to a standard-library function
  that takes one is lent and takes no word: after `xs.iter().for_each(h)`, `h` is the caller's still
findings.question: A program declares its own `owns f: F` exactly as std's `for_each` does. Does a named function given to it take `owns` and end, or is it lent as in std?
findings.why_unsettled: The same first line, `owns f: F`, means "lent, no word" when std wrote it and "handed over, `owns` at the call or E3028" when the program wrote it (GRM-15). So a written declaration's meaning depends on which package wrote it: a hidden special path (checklist 13 and 15). Verdict 150 names only the standard library. The spec never says whether `for_each(owns h)` is allowed in std, or how a library outside std gets the loan.
findings.searched: Spec: FN-2a, STD-19 (6709-6712), GRM-15, verdict notes (12639); JOB verdicts 147, 150, 158; decisions N36 ("for the standard library's functions only ... D-963").
findings.fix_idea: Base the loan on what the declaration says, not on who wrote it. Either every `[F: needs fn(..)]` parameter a function only calls lends a named function, in any package, or std's consumers take plain `f: F`. The owner must choose, since verdict 150 is his.

findings.quote:
(`[STD-19]`). An argument for a `Mutex`, `RwLock` or `Atomic` parameter, or a channel end, takes no word, since its own "only me" is
  the lock's block (`E3028`: "`top` takes the lock of `scores` itself; a `Mutex` takes no word at the
  call: `top(scores)`").
findings.question: When a channel end or a `Mutex` goes to an `owns` (or `ref mut`) parameter, is the call `start_worker(owns rx)` or `start_worker(rx)`? Which form is E3028?
findings.why_unsettled: FN-2a exempts these types from every call word. GRM-15 (verdict 147) requires `owns` before any argument for an `owns` parameter, whatever is given. Verdict 3's reason for the exemption is about `ref mut` only ("only me for the whole call" would be untrue). Handing a receiving end to a worker is a real hand-over: the caller's `rx` ends. With no word, nothing in the line shows that it ends. The same question arises for `ref mut m: Mutex[T]`, through which the callee may replace the caller's mutex.
findings.searched: Spec: FN-2a (2095), FN-1 (2059), GRM-15 (957-972), BRW-15 (3259), THR rules (5480-5512); grep for owns parameters of Sender/Receiver/Mutex/Atomic (none). JOB verdicts 3, 36, 37, 147.
findings.fix_idea: Narrow the exemption to what verdict 3 decided: a plain (read) parameter of these types takes no word. An `owns` one takes `owns` at the call as every argument does (`start_worker(owns rx)`), and a `ref mut` one takes `ref mut`.

findings.quote:
* `[CLS-3]` A class with no `init` and no base class gets a memberwise constructor as a struct does.
* `[CLS-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* A derived class with no `init` gets its base's constructor: `Door(entity)`
  evaluates `Door`'s field defaults and then runs `Script.init(entity)`.
findings.question: A base class has no `init`, so it has a memberwise constructor. What does a derived class's `super.init(…)` call, and does a derived class with no `init` get the base's memberwise constructor?
findings.why_unsettled: CLS-4 says a derived `init` MUST call `super.init(…)` exactly once, and CLS-11 orders it. But a base with no `init` has no `init` to call: CLS-3 gives a memberwise constructor only to a class with no `init` and no base. CLS-10's example assumes the base declares `init`. findings.searched: Spec: grep `super.init` (2305, 2308, 8439, 9585-9590 for C++ bases only), `memberwise` (1997, 2187, 2292); CLS-2, CLS-10, CLS-11, E2101, E2102.

findings.question: Does `take_hit(PLAYER)` print 10 or 9? And does `append_moved(ref mut keys, keys[0], 1.0)` compile? Both answers currently depend on how big the struct is and on the target's pointer size.
findings.example:
@derive(Copy)
struct Stats:
    hp: int
    armor: int

static mut PLAYER: Stats = Stats(hp=10, armor=2)

fn take_hit(s: Stats):
    PLAYER.hp -= 1
    println(s.hp)          # 10 if `s` went in registers, 9 if it was passed by address

@derive(Copy)
struct Transform:
    x: float
    y: float
    z: float
    angle: float           # 32 bytes: passed by address ([BRW-8])

fn append_moved(ref mut keys: Array[Transform], base: Transform, dx: float):
    keys.push(owns Transform(x=base.x + dx, y=base.y, z=base.z, angle=base.angle))

fn main():
    take_hit(PLAYER)
    keys: Array[Transform] = [Transform(x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0, angle=0.0)]
    append_moved(ref mut keys, keys[0], 1.0)   # accepted like [BRW-3]'s int case, or E3021?
findings.why_unsettled: [BRW-8] passes a plain `Copy` parameter in registers when it is at most two pointers and by address otherwise, and says the choice "cannot be observed". [FN-1] says the same ("the meaning is the same") and promises that what `a` reads does not change while `a` is used. But [BRW-21] and [BCK-8] check a plain parameter at the call only for end or move, and [BRW-21] says "Writing a number or a `bool` ends and moves nothing". The lead's area-2 Q4 ruling agrees: only end or move is checked, and "the compiler never assumes the value unchanged". So `take_hit(PLAYER)` compiles, and what it prints depends on the ABI choice: 10 when `Stats` (16 bytes) goes in registers on a 64-bit target, 9 when it goes by address on a 32-bit target. The second call shows the same thing at compile time. [BRW-3] accepts `f(ref mut v, v[0])` for an `int` "because `v[0]` is copied in". For `Transform`, which goes by address, `keys[0]` is a view held by an argument and overlaps `ref mut keys`, so [BRW-11] gives E3021. Whether the program compiles then depends on the struct's size and the target.

Also read decisions.md §4 (area 2 Q4) and JOB.md verdicts 5, 18 and 53. No rule holds a plain parameter to [BRW-1]'s promise against a number written by another name at the call, and none makes a large `Copy` parameter a copy.

Either a plain parameter of a `Copy` type is a copy taken at the call (as [FN-1] says for a number), with by-address only as an unobservable optimisation; or the call check holds a plain parameter to [BRW-1]'s promise, so that a callee's write by another name to what the parameter views while it is used is refused at the call, as it already is for `ref mut`.

findings.question: Where does an object given to a `retained` C parameter carry the mark that makes a later hand-over to another thread stop the program?
findings.example:
class Names:
    items: Array[String] = []

fn main():
    names = Names()
    register(names)                      # a C contract that keeps the address: param(names, retained)
    w = weakref names
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns names: names.items.len())   # stops ([THR-2], [FFI-35a]): C keeps its address
findings.why_unsettled: `[FFI-35a]` (verdict 114, fix 3) says such an object "is marked in its header as kept by C and never moves". decisions.md section 6 says the header has the room. `[OBJ-1]` says an object carries no flags but a `thread_shared` value's three marks, and its layout (count, type index, weak count) has no field for one. The header is part of the runtime ABI (`[VER-4]`), so the layout and the rule must agree.
findings.searched: OBJ-1/2/3 and the header tables in p08; FFI-35a (7272-7276), THR-2 (5430-5452), RT-3/10 in the assembled spec; decisions.md section 6 row [FFI-35a]; JOB.md verdict 114 (fix 3).
findings.fix_idea: Give the "kept by C" mark its place in `[OBJ-1]`'s layout and list it next to the three marks. Or keep it outside the header (a set the runtime keeps of retained objects) and say so in `[FFI-35a]`.

findings.quote:

findings.question: On a `thread_shared` value's making thread, at which count does making another owner stop the program: 2,147,483,647 or 4,294,967,295? And what does the 8-bit test print, 127 or 255?
findings.why_unsettled: `[RC-1]` says a `thread_shared` count stops at the lower limit (2,147,483,647). `[RC-4]` and `[RT-7]` say the home count "keep[s] the exact compare" and "is checked as a one-thread count is", that is at 4,294,967,295. Yet `[RT-7]`'s 8-bit test gives 127 for a `thread_shared` value. With the higher limit, the hand-over of `[RC-4]` point 4 adds a home count of up to 4,294,967,295 into the away count, whose limit is 2,147,483,647, and that add is not a checked +1.

findings.quote:
(`[LT-1]`, `[LT-44]`). `reset()`, `scope()` (`[ARN-6]`) and the arena's end may reuse or free that
memory: each ends every view into the arena, and a later use of one is `E3060`.
findings.question: Is a view allocated from the arena before `frame.scope()` still usable during and after the scope? Is `return root.kind` below E3060?
findings.example:
@derive(Zeroable)
struct Tok:
    kind: int

struct Node:
    kind: int

fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=1))   # kept for the whole parse
    with s = frame.scope():                          # scratch memory, released last in first out
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        toks[0].kind = 2
    return root.kind                                 # E3060 by [ARN-1], though the scope never touched root's bytes
findings.why_unsettled: `[ARN-1]` gives as its reason that `scope()` "may reuse or free that memory". `[ARN-6]` says a scope releases only what was allocated from it, last in first out, and `[ARN-1]` itself says views point into the memory, not the cursor. So `scope()` and its end never reuse bytes below the scope's mark, and the stated reason is untrue for views made before the scope. The rule as written refuses a correct program, the common arena layout of persistent nodes plus scratch scopes. It also leaves open whether using such a view inside the scope is "using the parent" (E3096).
findings.searched: ARN-1/6/7, ALC-5, LT-44 in p09 and the assembled spec; grep 'ScopedArena', '.scope()', 'E3096' (only ARN-6, LT-44, the code table, shape A1); JOB.md (no verdict on arena scopes).
findings.fix_idea: `scope()` and its end should end only the views made from that scope (the end lowers the pointer only to the scope's mark). Views made from the parent before it stay usable, and reading them is not "using the parent".

jobs.notes:
Patterns across the findings. (1) Several rules say "of that type" or "values of one type" where subtyping (base classes, `dyn I`) has to count: RC-5 point 1, WK-17 condition 2, BCK-7, DRP-8, BRW-17 and BCK-3. EXC-3 alone uses "class family", and even it accepts "different classes" as proof that two paths differ (J5-03, J5-04). One general rule would settle all of them. (2) Memory managers (`using`) have not been checked against links and threads: weakref blocks outliving the instance (J5-02), thread_shared values in a manager (J5-05), the Alloc effect of `using` (J5-11), String missing from the list of types `using` may follow (J5-09). (3) Library listings (CELL-1, ARN-5c/5d, STD-15) write parameters with no word, so verdict 147's call word cannot be read from them (J5-15).

Checked and found settled (not reported): `shares p` from a loop name or a `shares` parameter (OWN-13 covers it); a class field handed out (OWN-11, E3013, verdict 78); moving an object into its own subtree (BCK-4, BRW-11); `@packed` and `@align` on classes (the attribute table says struct and enum only); a final class (CLS-4); Cell being Copy while built on UnsafeCell (Cell is compiler-declared, line 1674).

Left out as weak or belonging to other parts; the later reviewers should know:
- WK-15 says an object in the leak report "was kept by unsafe code or by foreign code". CT-5 says "statics are never dropped", and it is unclear whether that covers `static mut` values built on first access. So whether a class object held in a `static mut` has its `drop` run at exit, or is reported as leaked, is open (Part V / STA).
- RC-3's `with h:` and `mem.keep_alive(h)` have no meaning defined anywhere: the grammar has `with_item` only, and `mem.keep_alive` gets no signature.
- E3032's help (WK-6, shape B17, and verdict 99's own text) suggests `next: Option[weakref Node]`. WK-11 already lets a `weakref` hold none, so that type is doubly optional: `exists as` gives the link, not the node.
- ARN-11: whether an enum with a valid zero discriminant can be `Zeroable` (by derive or automatically), and whether `unsafe extend T implements Zeroable` by hand is allowed.
- What a `using` making line does when `allocate` returns null (ALC-2) is not stated; ALC-4 covers only standard containers.
- Wording slips: OBJ-4 says "the memory manager the class names with `using`", but the place names it (ALC-1). DSP-4 omits `shares mut dyn I`, which TYP-44 lists. ARN-6 cites LT-46 for a `ref mut` view, where ARN-4 cites LT-45.

Not checked in depth: the WK-17 and WK-18 proofs (optimisations with no observable effect); WK-4, WK-8, WK-9, CLI-18, RC-6 and SEL-1 (tooling, outside the brief).

The effect table defines Unsafe as 'the body contains unsafe', and EFF-1 unions every effect over callees. findings.question: May a program make a `weakref` link to a class object held in a `static`, from one thread or from several? If it may, where is the weak count kept, given that CT-5 puts the object in read-only memory and WK-11 counts every link in the target's header?

findings.fix_idea: Make a `weakref` (and `sharedref mut`) to an object held in a static a compile error with its own code (a static never ends, so `ref` is the link to use), as verdict 103 does for `shares`; or keep class-object statics out of read-only memory and count their links atomically.

findings.question: Which operation carries `Nondet` for 'thread and job completion order'? In the example, which line, if any, is E4070?
findings.example:
static ORDER_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
static mut ORDER: Array[int] guarded by ORDER_LOCK = []

fn push_one():
    with ORDER_LOCK:
        ORDER.push(owns 1)

fn push_two():
    with ORDER_LOCK:
        ORDER.push(owns 2)

@deterministic
fn race() -> Array[int]:
    a = thread.spawn(push_one)
    b = thread.spawn(push_two)
    a.join()
    b.join()
    with ORDER_LOCK:
        return copy of ORDER       # [1, 2] or [2, 1]
findings.why_unsettled: DET-2 claims to list Nondet's sources 'exactly', but 'completion order' is not an operation: it does not say whether spawn, join, taking a lock, a channel `recv` with several senders, `try_lock`, `try_recv` or an Atomic's `fetch_add` result carries it. It cannot be spawn, because THR-21 keeps a reduction of scoped tasks free of Nondet. A lockstep simulation needs to know which of these lines refuses.
findings.searched: Spec: every `Nondet` mention (4968, 5193-5211, 5748, 5816, 6277, 6294, 6460, 6612, 6902, 6908), THR-15 (channels), THR-21. JOB.md verdicts 92 and 105 (reductions only).
findings.fix_idea: Name the operations: taking a lock that another thread may also take, `recv`/`try_recv` on a channel with more than one sender, `try_lock`, and an atomic read-modify-write whose result is used carry Nondet; spawn and join do not (THR-21 stays as written).

findings.quote:
`std` is layered, and each layer depends only on the ones before it: **core** (scalars,
  `Option`, `Result`, views, fixed-capacity containers, math, SIMD), **alloc** (`Array`, `String`,
  `Map`, `Set`, and the heap blocks of `owns` and `shares` values)
findings.question: Can a package with `layers = ["core"]` write `-> Result[int]` (whose error type defaults to `AnyError`), or `AnyError` at all?
findings.why_unsettled: STD-6's table puts AnyError in std.core, and ERR-9 makes it the default error parameter of every `Result[T]`. But AnyError is an `owns dyn Error` held in a heap block, and its `?` conversion allocates (ERR-8, ERR-11); heap blocks of `owns` values belong to the alloc layer. BLD-11 bars a core-only package from alloc. So either the firmware package's plain `Result[int]` is refused (with an unclear code), or the core layer allocates.
findings.searched: Spec: STD-6, the module table (6447-6467), BLD-11 (7931), ODR-151 (10685), ERR-8/9/11, the prelude table (2014). JOB.md has no verdict.

findings.question: For an `owns` parameter of a function type, do `b.on_click(beep)` (the program's own method) and `b.handlers.push(beep)` (std's `push`, which keeps what it is given) compile without `owns`? Is `beep` still the caller's afterwards?
findings.example:
type Handler = fn()

class Button:
    handlers: Array[Handler] = []

    fn on_click(owns f: Handler):
        this.handlers.push(owns f)

fn main():
    b = Button()
    beep = fn(): println("beep")
    b.handlers.push(beep)   # std function given a function from a variable: lent?
    b.on_click(beep)        # same parameter in the program's own code: E3028?
    beep()
findings.why_unsettled: Verdict 150 (FN-2a at spec 2093) lends a function from a variable only when it is given to a standard-library function. So one parameter declaration (`owns f: F` or `owns f: Handler`) means 'lent' in std and 'say owns' (verdict 147) in the program's own code, a hidden special path for the library (STD-9 calls std functions 'ordinary functions of the library'). It is also undecided for std functions that keep the value: a list cannot hold a lent function past the call, so `handlers.push(beep)` is either an E3028, a silent hand-over, or a view stored in a list.
findings.fix_idea: Base the rule on what the parameter does, not where it lives. A function from a variable is lent with no word to any parameter whose function is called only during the call (a type parameter `F`, for std or the program's own code). A parameter that keeps the value (push, a field) needs `owns beep` or `owns copy of beep`, as verdict 147 says.

findings.question: Does `who.trim() in names` compile for `names: Array[String]` (and `"bob" in names`)? If so, does the literal allocate a String for the test?
findings.example:
fn main():
    names: Array[String] = ["ana", "bob"]
    who = input("name? ")
    if who.trim() in names:        # StrView in Array[String]
        println("welcome back")
    if "bob" in names:             # literal: StrView, or a new String (TXT-9)?
        println("bob is here")
findings.why_unsettled: `Set[String]` and `Map[String, V]` take any `Q: needs AsKey[K]`, so a StrView finds a String key (STD-12). STD-8 gives Array, Span and `[T; N]` only `Contains[T]`, so `who.trim() in names` is E2226 for a list and fine for a set, with no reason given. For a literal, TXT-9 makes it a String wherever a String is expected, but `x in c` does not say whether it expects `T`. That decides between E2226 and an allocation (Alloc, refused under @noalloc).
findings.searched: Spec: STD-8/8a/8b (6670-6679), STD-12, the Contains interface (1742-1743), the collection literal rules (2626-2644), TXT-9. JOB.md has no verdict.
findings.fix_idea: Give the linear-scan containers `Contains[Q]` for every `Q: needs AsKey[T]`, as Map and Set have, so a StrView or literal is compared without making a String.

findings.question: Is `AnyError` `Send`? Does a worker thread that returns `Result[int]` compile? If AnyError is Send, may an error that holds a one-thread owner be converted into one?

findings.quote: **A `drop` runs where the last owner ends.** The last owner of a `thread_shared` value may end on any thread that holds a / 3. **Check points.** The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may
findings.question: When a queued `thread_shared` value is ended at its making thread's check point (a loop's back edge), its `drop` runs there. Does the program below compile, and if it does, what stops the drop from taking a lock this thread holds, or from pushing to the list this loop walks?
findings.example:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns this.id)

class Batch:
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())   # Conn travels inside b: no hand-over (RC-4 point 5)
    with pool.lock:
        for id in pool.free:          # back edge = check point; the queued Conn's drop runs here
            println(id)
    h.join()
findings.why_unsettled: THR-20 says a drop runs where the last owner ends and charges it to the function on the other thread. RC-4 points 2 and 5 and WK-3 say otherwise: a value that was not handed over is ended by its making thread at its next check point, and "its `drop` runs there". Check points sit at every loop back edge and before every blocking call, so the drop of any queued value can run in the middle of a walk (BRW-18), inside a held lock (THR-19 promises "nothing checked while the program runs" for such waits, but this one would hang for ever), or inside a @nolock/@realtime function (EFF-6 checks only the drop glue it can see). No rule counts these drops in the making thread's summary, and none keeps check points out of lock blocks or walks.
findings.searched: Whole spec for 'check point' (RC-4 at 4074-4104, WK-3 at 4285, RT-10 at 8966, OBJ-1, the cost table at 5252), THR-19, THR-20, EFF-1/EFF-24/EFF-25, BRW-18, and JOB.md verdict 101 (which says only that the making thread deletes it at its next check point)
findings.fix_idea: Count a check point as possibly ending every `thread_shared` type this thread makes and hands out inside other objects, so their drops enter the summary (E3020/E7018/contracts apply). Or place no check point inside a lock's `with` block or a walk, and run queued drops only at check points outside them.

findings.quote: 3. **Check points.** The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may / block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread / ends. A value whose making thread has ended is ended at once by the thread that ends its last
findings.question: A value made on a job worker, or on a host thread that has gone back into C, is queued to that thread, which runs no compiled Ember code and so reaches no check point. When does its `drop` run? Ever? And does the main thread's end, a check point, run queued drops, when THR-16 says no drop runs once `main` returns?
findings.why_unsettled: RC-4 point 3 has the compiler place check points in compiled code, plus 'when the thread ends'. Two kinds of thread stay alive without running Ember code: a job worker idle in the runtime's wait, and a host thread attached through FFI-22 that has returned to C. A value whose making thread is one of these waits without bound, so its drop (closing a file, giving back a GPU resource) may never run, and RC-3 says a value is ended 'never earlier' but sets no latest time. Separately, THR-16 says no drop runs when `main` returns, while point 3 places a check point when the thread ends, which drops values queued to main.
findings.searched: RC-4, RT-8/RT-10, THR-16, XI.5 intro and JOB-1..5, HR-3a (thread registration), FFI-22 by grep, JOB.md verdict 101
findings.fix_idea: Have the runtime run a check point whenever a worker goes idle and whenever a host thread leaves Ember code (the depth counter of HR-42 reaching zero). Say whether main's end runs queued drops before THR-16's exit.

findings.quote: `Send`; a `thread_shared T`, and a `weakref` link to one, when `T` is `Send` and `ThreadShared`; / `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`). Of the function types, `thread_shared fn()` is / `Send` (`[THR-1]`).
findings.question: Is `thread_shared X()` refused when `X` is `Send` but not `ThreadShared`? Does the program below compile (two threads set one `Cell` under read guards)?
findings.example:
import std.thread
from std.sync import RwLock

class Cache:
    hits: RwLock[Cell[int]] = RwLock(Cell(0))

fn bump(c: thread_shared Cache):
    with g = c.hits.read():
        g.set(g.get() + 1)

fn main():
    c = thread_shared Cache()
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared c: bump(c))
    bump(c)
    h.join()
findings.why_unsettled: THR-1's checks at the line that makes a value `thread_shared` are E7015 (everything reachable must be `Send`) and E7014 (state changes only through an Atomic, Mutex, RwLock, ...). Neither asks for `ThreadShared`. THR-9 itself says `RwLock[Cell[int]]` is not `ThreadShared`, but nothing refuses it inside a `thread_shared` object. THR-8 makes `thread_shared T` `Send` only for a `ThreadShared` T, yet `thread_shared fn()` is `Send` unconditionally, and THR-1 lets it hold any `thread_shared` owner. So `thread.spawn` accepts it, and two threads change the Cell at once: a data race THR-13 says cannot happen.
findings.searched: THR-1, THR-8, THR-9, TYP-43's table (lines 1667-1668), CELL-3, RC-7, OWN-13 and every 'ThreadShared' hit in the assembled spec; JOB.md verdicts 61, 94, 101
findings.fix_idea: At the line that makes a value `thread_shared`, require `T` to be `Send` and `ThreadShared` (E7015, naming the component that is not, as `Bus.handlers` is named), which matches THR-8's condition for the owner.

findings.quote: A task makes, ends / or opens a `weakref` link only to a `thread_shared` target, and makes no `shares` owner (`[THR-2]`).
findings.question: May a scoped task end a `shares` owner, or end an object that `weakref` links may reach? Both change the object's header with plain arithmetic while the parent may be counting the same header. Does this compile?
findings.example:
import std.thread

class Enemy:
    hp: int = 10

class Level:
    enemies: Array[shares mut Enemy] = []

fn main():
    boss = shares mut Enemy()
    level = Level(enemies=[shares mut boss])
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): level.enemies.clear())   # task: plain -1 on boss's count
        hud_target = shares mut boss                    # parent: plain +1 on the same count, at once
        println(hud_target.hp)
    println(boss.hp)
findings.why_unsettled: For `weakref` the rule restricts a task's making, ending and opening of links. For `shares` it restricts only making an owner. A task that ends one (`clear`, replacing a field, a local's end) changes a one-thread count with a plain subtract. The parent, touching other places (`boss`, `hud_target`), may make or end owners of the same object at the same moment, and E7007 compares places, not headers. The same holds when a task ends a one-owner object with `weakref` links (OBJ-3 decrements its weak count and marks it ended) while the parent opens or makes a link to it. THR-2's list of routes names unscoped threads, jobs and `thread_shared fn()`, not scoped tasks, and RC-7 defers to §XI.3, which says only 'makes no shares owner'.
findings.searched: THR-2, THR-11, THR-13 bullets, THR-21, RC-1, RC-4, RC-7 (line 4051), OBJ-3, WK-12, LT-46, E7007/E7015 table rows; JOB.md verdicts 77, 93, 94, 104, 114
findings.fix_idea: Give `shares` the `weakref` rule's symmetry: a task makes or ends no `shares` owner and ends no object that `weakref` links may reach, unless it is `thread_shared` (E7015, with the line that makes it `thread_shared`). Or treat ending an object of type T in a task as changing every place that may reach a T, for E7007.

findings.question: A type that holds a raw pointer to a thread-safe C object can be vouched `Send` but never `ThreadShared` (E2040). Does the program below compile, and if it does not, how does a program let several threads read such a value?

    raw: *mut c_logger      # c_logger locks internally

# SAFETY: every c_logger function takes its own lock
unsafe extend CLogger implements Send:

static LOGGER: CLogger = CLogger(raw=null)    # STA-1: T MUST be ThreadShared -> E7002

fn log_all(lg: CLogger, lines: Span[String]):
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for t in lines:
            scope.spawn(owns fn() ref t: c_log(lg, t))   # needs `ref CLogger` Send, i.e. CLogger ThreadShared

findings.question: What does a task's private accumulator (or a chunk's 'own copy' in PAR-3) start from, and how is it combined for `-=` on an unsigned field, for `*=`, and for one task that mixes `+=` and `*=` on one place? What does the program below print, or does it stop?

import std.thread

class Player:
    hp: u8 = 10

fn main():
    p = Player()
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): p.hp -= 1)
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): p.hp -= 2)
    println(p.hp)        # one by one: 7. An accumulator of type u8 starting at 0 stops at 0 - 1.
findings.why_unsettled: THR-21 says the accumulator 'has the place's type' and its operations are checked as the place's are, but never gives its first value or the combining operation per operator. For `-=` on an unsigned type, an accumulator that starts at 0 and subtracts overflows on the first change, though the one-by-one result (7) fits, and verdict 105's 'equal when no task's total overflows' does not say whether the task's total is -1 or 1. PAR-3's 'each chunk has its own copy' can be read as a copy of the variable's value, so a `total` of 100 before the loop would be added once per chunk. A task that both adds and multiplies one place has no single private accumulator that combines in spawn order.
findings.searched: THR-21, THR-13, PAR-3, PAR-5, glossary 'reduction' (10001), cost row (5286); JOB.md verdicts 77, 92, 105

Safe code can fill such a struct with `ref_to_ptr` (safe, ODR-075) and any length, and C then reads or writes through it.
findings.why_unsettled: FFI-10 refuses a raw pointer as a `safe fn` parameter ("complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter ... safe to expose"). Wrapped in a `@layout(c)` value type, the same pointer passes the list. Contract words attach only to parameters, and FFI-30a forbids an overlay from touching fields, so no contract can state a field's count or lifetime. The spec's own overlay asserts `vkCreateBuffer(pCreateInfo: borrowed one)`, whose struct holds `pQueueFamilyIndices` and its count.
findings.searched: Assembled spec FFI-10 (6969-7020), FFI-56 (7501-7512), UNS-1, ODR-075 (1431, 10609), FFI-30a, holds no pointer / pointer field
findings.fix_idea: Extend FFI-10's raw-pointer rule to a `@layout(c)` type reached by value or through a contracted pointer: one with a raw pointer field makes `safe fn` E5002 (and `@ffi(safe)` likewise), unless the field's facts can be stated.

FFI-56 makes every function pointer that comes from C ("an argument C passes to a callback") an `unsafe extern "C" fn`, and E5054 refuses `char` because C may pass a value no `char` holds.

pub extern "C" fn game_log(msg: CStrView, done: extern "C" fn(i32)) -> i32:

The reason given for E5054 (C may pass any `uint32_t`) applies to a null or unterminated `const char*` too.

Examples are a header-only library, an `inline` variable with a dynamic initializer, or `<iostream>`'s static initializer, all of which run before `main`.

FFI-11 gives a `retained` non-callback pointer no safe type (the call stays unsafe, with a raw pointer). jobs.notes: Pattern: most gaps come from Part XVI's C rules not being applied to Annex C's C++ imports, or the reverse. Examples: FFI-2a's underived result lifetime against FFI-40's derived `T&` result (J8-06), C vs C++ const globals (J8-07), FFI-51's `unsafe import` for code compiled into the program (J8-11), and destructors for adopt (J8-16). A second pattern: hand declarations (FFI-10) say how a `safe fn` writes count witnesses and nullable spans (ODR-074..080) but not callbacks and user_data (J8-01), nor `handle` types (J8-14). The overlay grammar (GRM-35) cannot name C++ overloads or operators (J8-04, J8-05). Checked and settled, not reported: FFI-16 with one `out` (assembled line 11347 gives the one output's type; tuples need two or more, ODR-071); FFI-24b panic vs FFI-39e abort (PAN-1 aborts); verdict 120's @safety on extern functions (UNS-7 restricts it to `unsafe fn`, consistent with verdict 136); verdict 39's `changes` clauses (voided by verdict 86); verdicts 121, 123, 125, 127, 130-133 and 136 are carried.
